meta.title: Vietnamese C1 Advanced
meta.subtitle: 1500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Vietnamese → English (see the Vietnamese, recall the meaning) and English → Vietnamese (see an English meaning, recall the Vietnamese). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1500 words for an advanced learner, aligned to C1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand a wide range of demanding, longer texts, and recognise implicit meaning' — a learner here is able to express ideas fluently and spontaneously without much obvious searching for expressions, to use language flexibly and effectively for social, academic and professional purposes, and to produce clear, well-structured, detailed text on complex subjects. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Vietnam's own framework for learners of Vietnamese publishes no graded word list, and neither does any exam board, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 156 of the 1500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — philosophy and ethics, religion and the inner life, academic and scholarly Vietnamese, government, diplomacy and the constitution, the economy and development, medicine and the body, law and rights, language and literature, the shades of feeling and judgement, the Sino-Vietnamese abstract nouns and adjectives of formal prose, and the literary connectors and adverbs — and the other 1344 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Vietnamese, counted in film and television subtitles. Vietnamese writes a space between syllables rather than between words, so the subtitles were divided into words against the dictionary first, and a two-syllable word such as học sinh (pupil) is counted as one word. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Beneath every headword its tones are named, one per syllable — ngang (no mark), huyền (à), sắc (á), hỏi (ả), ngã (ã) and nặng (ạ) — read off the marks the word is spelt with. 138 nouns show their classifier, the word that stands between a number and the noun (hai con mèo, two cats), and 579 words borrowed from Chinese show the characters they come from. The pronunciation is given in IPA for Hanoi and, where it differs, for Saigon. Real example sentences come with 824 of the 1500 words, three apiece for 357 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Spellings are Wiktionary's, which often puts the tone mark in the older place (hoà, khoẻ); the newer (hòa, khỏe) is equally correct. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, classifiers, characters and pronunciation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the OpenSubtitles 2018 Vietnamese text (opensubtitles.org, via the OPUS corpus collection), counted here. Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
